claims.text: HEA protective coatings reduce wear primarily through dynamic formation of a self-renewing, passivating oxide tribolayer at the wear interface.
Alloying additions can accelerate the formation kinetics of the oxide tribolayer.
The oxide tribolayer protects the underlying coating from direct mechanical damage.
The baseline is a uniform multi-principal-element HEA coating designed for wear resistance.
The controlled intervention is an approximately 5 at% addition of Cr or Al to the baseline coating.
Cr or Al acts as an oxidation-promoting addition in this coating.
An approximately 5 at% Cr or Al addition can accelerate protective-oxide formation without substantially altering other bulk properties.
The relevant mediator is a coherent oxide tribolayer that is continuously regenerated during wear.
The added element accelerates surface oxidation under high-stress sliding.
Accelerated surface oxidation causes rapid formation and repair of a protective oxide film.
The protective oxide film reduces direct asperity contact.
Reduced asperity contact minimizes material removal and decreases wear rate.
The modified coating is expected to have a lower wear rate than the baseline coating.
The modified coating is expected to have a lower friction coefficient than the baseline coating.
The modified coating is expected to form a thicker or more uniform oxide tribolayer than the baseline coating.
The baseline coating may have slower or less effective intrinsic oxidation kinetics than the modified coating.
The proposed mechanism should operate at moderate to high temperatures and under cyclic sliding when oxidation is sufficiently active to form a protective layer.
Direct in situ evidence linking accelerated oxide formation to reduced wear in HEA coatings has not yet been reported.
Failure of the modified coating to show both a statistically significant wear-rate reduction and improved oxide-tribolayer formation relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
